transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I, uh... I guess I’m here because things have gotten really, really complicated at work lately. I’m a transportation inspector, you know, making sure the county transit vehicles are up to code, checking maintenance logs, all that. And I take my job seriously. I’m good at it. Actually, a little while back, I won this county safety award. It was a big deal, I caught a major brake line issue before it caused a pileup. But, honestly, ever since they handed me that plaque, it’s like... it’s like it put this massive target on my back. 

Certain people at the depot—and I won't name names right this second, but I know exactly who they are—they’ve been taking my inspection reports and completely twisting them around. They pull me aside and ask these incredibly pointed budget questions, scrutinizing every single line item like they’re trying to make me look crooked, like I'm skimming or faking the numbers or something. 

And I went to my supervisor about it, I laid it all out for him, and he just... he brushes it off. He tells me, 'Oh, it’s just a normal review, everyone goes through it, don't worry.' But I’ve been doing this for years, I know what a normal review looks like, and this isn't it. Not even close. I can tell, just by the way the emails are worded and how they look at me when I walk into the dispatch office, there is a coordinated effort to discredit me. They want me out, and it’s... well, it’s why I’m sitting here, because dealing with this constant plotting behind my back is just... it's a lot to handle on my own.
Are you certain that your coworkers are deliberately trying to discredit you?

Am I certain? Doc, I am... I mean, absolutely, one hundred percent certain. You don't just imagine this kind of thing. Like I was saying, it all started literally the week after that county safety award banquet. Before that, everything was fine, I was just a regular guy doing his job, keeping the buses on the road. But the second I got that plaque, it's like a switch flipped. 

I'll give you a perfect example. Just last Tuesday, I submitted a standard Form 4-B on a brake pad replacement for Bus 402. Completely standard stuff, I've filled out hundreds of them. Two days later, they pull me into this little glass office—the one by the vending machines where everyone in the breakroom can see you—and they start grilling me on why the parts requisition took an extra twelve dollars. Twelve dollars! They were asking these incredibly pointed budget questions, looking at me over their clipboards like I'm running some kind of black market parts ring out of the garage, just really trying to make me look crooked. 

And it's not just the money, they take my actual inspection notes, the ones I write meticulously, and they completely twist the wording around. Like, if I write 'monitor rear suspension for future wear,' they try to spin it in the system to say I 'ignored an active hazard.' It's insane. It's a deliberate twisting of my words. 

And then I go to my supervisor, I literally put the emails right on his desk. I printed them out, I highlighted the discrepancies, I showed him the timestamps, everything. I laid out the whole pattern. And he just sighs, leans back in his chair, and gives me this canned corporate line. 'Oh, it's just a normal review, everyone goes through it, don't worry about it.' But I know everyone doesn't go through it! I've been working there since I was twenty-two, right out of high school basically, and nobody gets grilled like this unless management is trying to build a paper trail to fire them. I can tell, I can just feel it in the room, the way the dispatchers stop talking when I walk in... there is absolutely a coordinated effort to discredit me. They want to ruin my reputation so they can push me out, and I am absolutely certain of it. You'd have to be blind not to see the pieces moving.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Voices? Like... like people who aren't there? No, doc, no. I know why you're asking that, I mean, you're a psychiatrist, you have to run down the checklist, right? Make sure I'm not, you know, totally losing my grip or hallucinating. But no, absolutely not. The things I'm hearing... the conversations I'm talking about, they are coming from actual, physical people standing right there in the depot. It's not in my head. 

Like, okay, our breakroom at the garage has these super thin drywall partitions—the cheap kind they threw up back in the nineties when they expanded the dispatch center—and you can hear practically everything through them. So when I say I hear them talking, I don't mean some spooky disembodied voices or whatever. I mean I can literally hear Dave from scheduling or Mike, the lead mechanic, standing by the coffee maker—the big industrial one that always leaks a little water on the linoleum—and they are actually whispering about my reports. I hear real words from real people. 

Actually, my hearing is perfect. I had to do a full DOT physical and an audiogram when I got promoted to inspector, and I scored top marks on the high-frequency tones. So maybe that's the problem, really. They think they're keeping their voices down, they think they're being so slick whispering behind the vending machines, but I can hear the actual sound of them trying to set me up. But voices when no one is there? No, never. If I hear someone talking, you better believe there's a guy in a county uniform standing right there doing the talking.
Has anyone told you that your speech is hard to follow or that your thoughts seem jumbled?

Hard to follow? Jumbled? No, no, definitely not. I mean, if anything, I’m the one who has to constantly clarify things for everyone else. You know how it is in county government, right? You get these memos that are just total word salad, all this bureaucratic jargon—'synergizing maintenance protocols' and 'optimizing operational bandwidth.' It’s nonsense. I'm the guy who actually reads the manual, understands the code, and communicates it clearly. 

I mean, look, when I write an inspection report, it is crystal clear. I use bullet points, I reference the exact section of the safety manual—like Section 4, Paragraph B, regarding hydraulic fluid viscosity—I lay it all out logically. My thoughts are perfectly organized. I have to be organized to do my job, to keep track of all the different buses, the maintenance schedules, the parts inventory. If my thoughts were jumbled, I’d be approving vehicles with faulty steering columns or missing brake pads, and I don't do that. I catch the things other people miss because my mind works in a very systematic, logical way. 

No one has ever told me I'm hard to follow. Well, except maybe my supervisor, but that's only when I'm trying to explain the conspiracy to him, and he just doesn't want to hear it. He'll say, 'Slow down, you're jumping all over the place,' but I'm not jumping all over the place, I'm just trying to connect the dots for him! I'm trying to show him how the email from Dave on Tuesday connects to the missing requisition form on Thursday, and how that ties into the way Mike was looking at me in the breakroom on Friday. It's all connected, and I can explain it perfectly, step-by-step, but they just... they pretend it's confusing because they don't want to admit what's really going on. But my actual speech? My thoughts? No, they're sharp. They have to be. If I wasn't thinking clearly, they would have gotten rid of me by now. I have to stay ten steps ahead of them just to keep my job.
Do you believe anyone outside of your workplace is also trying to harm or plot against you?

Outside of work? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, why would they? My whole life, my whole routine, it really revolves around the depot. I get up, I go to the garage, I do my inspections, I come home. I don't really have a lot of hobbies or, you know, a huge social circle where people would even care enough to plot against me. I mean, I go to the grocery store—the one on 4th Street, usually on Sunday mornings when it's quiet—and nobody there is looking at me weird or following me down the cereal aisle or anything. The cashier, Linda, she's always perfectly nice, asks if I found everything okay. 

And my neighbors, they're fine. I live in this little apartment complex, just a bunch of people keeping to themselves. The guy across the hall plays his TV a little loud sometimes, usually sports, but it's not like he's doing it to mess with me, he's just older and probably losing his hearing. Nobody is, like, tapping my phone lines or watching my apartment. I mean, I check, obviously. When I pull into my parking spot, I take a look around, just a quick scan of the lot, make sure there are no strange cars idling, no county vehicles parked where they shouldn't be. But it's always just the usual cars—the blue Honda, the rusty pickup truck. 

So, no, the problem is entirely contained at the workplace. That's the arena. That's where the threat is. They want my job, they want to discredit my inspections, and they want me gone from the county transit authority. They don't care what I do on my own time, as long as I'm not in that garage finding their mistakes. They just want to push me out of the picture at work. So, yeah, outside of work, I feel totally fine. I can actually relax a little bit when I'm at home, you know? At least until Sunday night, when I have to start thinking about going back into that snake pit on Monday morning.
How long have you believed your coworkers were plotting against you?

Well, if you really want to pin down a timeline, it’s been about a year. Yeah, right around a year now. It all started—and I remember this clearly because of the timing—right after I got recognized for the county safety initiative. 

See, the county transit authority does this thing every spring, usually around April, where they roll out these new safety protocols and they recognize staff who go above and beyond. And last year, they handed me this certificate—it’s just a piece of paper, really, printed on that thick cardstock with the county seal stamped in the corner—because I caught a systemic issue with the pneumatic doors on the 40-foot hybrid buses. It was a huge deal. I mean, if those doors fail while the bus is in motion, you’re looking at a massive liability, potential passenger injury, a PR nightmare for the county. I documented the whole thing, submitted a 15-page report with photographs and schematics, and they had to pull twelve buses off the line to fix the actuators. 

They gave me a plaque at the monthly all-hands meeting. The director shook my hand. And I thought, you know, I thought it was a good thing. I thought I was doing my job and protecting the public. But that’s exactly when the temperature in the garage changed. That’s when the plotting started. 

Because, think about it, by finding that flaw, I made the maintenance guys look bad. I made Mike, the lead mechanic, look incompetent because his team missed it during their routine checks. And Dave in scheduling had to scramble to cover the routes for those twelve buses, which messed up his whole board for a month. So instead of saying, 'Hey, good catch, you saved us a lawsuit,' they started looking at me like I was the enemy. 

It started small. Like, right after the ceremony, maybe a week later, I noticed my inspection logs were being moved. Not thrown away, just... shifted on my desk. Just enough to let me know someone had been in my workspace. Then it escalated to the whispers in the breakroom, the sudden silence when I walked into the dispatch office. And it’s just been building and building for twelve months straight. Every single day for a year, I’ve had to watch my back, double-check my own locks on my tool chest, make copies of every single form I submit, because I know—I know for a fact—they are just waiting for me to slip up so they can get me fired and go back to running things their sloppy, dangerous way. So, yeah, a year. A whole year of this.
Apart from your coworkers plotting against you, have you had any other beliefs that other people say are strange or not true?

Other beliefs? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I'm a very grounded guy. The only thing people say is "not true" or "strange" is... well, it's exactly what I'm here for. It's the situation at work. 

Because, look, I’m here because ever since that county safety award—the one I was just telling you about with the pneumatic doors—certain people at work have been literally twisting my inspection reports. I’ll write a physical report, right? I'll note that a tie rod is showing early signs of fatigue, just standard preventative maintenance. I'll cite the manual. But then it goes up the chain, and suddenly it's being framed like I'm flagging perfectly good vehicles just to cause trouble and slow down the routes. 

And then come the budget questions. Oh, man, the budget questions. Out of nowhere, I've got people from procurement and administration asking me these incredibly pointed budget questions, demanding I justify the cost of the replacement parts I'm recommending.
If your supervisor showed you clear proof that the reviews and questions were routine and not directed at you, would you accept that?

Proof? What kind of proof could he possibly show me? Look, my supervisor, he’s—well, he’s part of the whole system, isn't he? He’s the one who sits me down and tells me, "Oh, it's just a normal review, everyone goes through this, it's standard operating procedure." Standard operating procedure. That's the phrase he uses, like it’s some kind of magic wand that makes the truth disappear. 

But I'm the one on the ground. I'm the one who sees the actual paperwork before it gets, you know, sanitized or whatever they do to it upstairs. I see how they take my reports—reports that are meticulously detailed, by the way, based on the manufacturer's own safety tolerances—and they twist them. They twist the narrative so it looks like I'm the problem. They make it seem like I'm just flagging things to be difficult or to drain the budget. And then they hit me with those budget questions. "Why are you recommending this part? Do you know how much this costs the county?" Like they’re trying to make me look crooked, like I'm getting kickbacks from the parts supplier or something ridiculous like that. 

So if my supervisor brings me a spreadsheet or an email chain and says, "See? Routine," I’m not just going to nod and say, "Okay, sure, I must be imagining things." Because I'm not. I know what's happening. Even when he sits there with a straight face and tells me it's normal, I can tell. I can read between the lines. I see the patterns. There is a coordinated effort to discredit me, to make me look like a liability so they can push me out and go back to ignoring safety standards. You can't just show me a piece of paper and expect me to unsee a whole year of them actively trying to ruin my reputation. It’s not just one person, it’s a coordinated thing, and no "proof" he fabricates is going to change the reality of what I experience every single day in that garage.
Has this situation at work caused your job performance to get worse?

Well, worse? No, I wouldn't say worse. I mean, my actual performance, the nuts and bolts of what I do, that hasn't slipped at all. If anything, I'm more thorough now, you know? Because I have to be. I still get to the garage right on time, 5:45 AM sharp, every single morning. I clock in, I grab my clipboard, I do my walk-arounds. I'm still completing every single inspection on my schedule. I haven't missed a day. I haven't let a single bus roll out of that depot if it wasn't up to code. 

And outside of work, I'm keeping it together, too. I still go to church on Sundays—I sit in the same pew, I talk to Pastor Dave, I help with the food drive. I'm eating right, making sure I get my sleep, keeping my apartment clean. I'm taking care of myself because I know I need to be sharp. I can't afford to be sloppy, not with them watching me the way they do. 

So, no, the performance itself is solid. The work is getting done, and it's getting done right. The problems... the problems only really flare up when there's an interaction about the work. Like, if I'm just under a bus checking the suspension, I'm fine. But the second I hand in the report and someone—whether it's Dave or Mike or some guy from procurement—comes up to me and starts questioning what I wrote? Or when they start bringing up those budget questions, asking me to justify why I'm recommending a $200 part to prevent a $10,000 breakdown? That's when things get tense. That's when the friction happens. Because I have to stand my ground, right? I have to defend the integrity of the inspection. So it might look to them like I'm being difficult or that my performance is an issue, but it's really just me refusing to back down when they try to corner me about my reports and my spending recommendations. The work itself? The work is flawless.
Have you ever felt that someone was putting thoughts into your mind or taking thoughts out of your mind?

Put thoughts into my mind? No, no, of course not. That's... I mean, that sounds like something out of a science fiction movie, right? Like telepathy or mind control or something. No, my thoughts are completely my own. I know exactly what I'm thinking, and I know why I'm thinking it. It's because of the facts, the evidence right in front of me at the depot. 

I mean, if someone could just put thoughts into my head, they wouldn't need to go through all this trouble, would they? They wouldn't need to twist my reports or send procurement down to grill me about the budget. They could just, I don't know, beam a thought into my brain that says, "Hey, ignore that worn tie rod, it's totally fine." But they can't do that, because that's impossible. My mind is clear. It's sharp. Like I said, I have to keep it sharp to stay ahead of what they're trying to pull. 

So, no, nobody is taking my thoughts or putting new ones in. Every thought I have about the safety protocols, about the pneumatic doors, about the way they're trying to frame me—it all comes from my own observations. From being on the ground, doing the work, and seeing exactly how they operate. My mind is 100% mine, Doc. That's the one thing they can't mess with, which is probably why they're trying so hard to mess with everything else on paper.
Before this started at work, were you generally a very distrustful or suspicious person?

Me? Distrustful? No, no, not at all. I mean, if you look at my track record before all this started, before I really started seeing what they were doing with the safety reports... I was probably the most trusting guy in the depot. 

Honestly, back when I was just starting out, right out of high school when I was a junior mechanic, I was the guy who would lend you my personal torque wrench or my diagnostic scanner and not even ask when you were going to give it back. I just trusted people. I figured, you know, we all come to work, we all want to do a good job, we fix the buses, we go home. Simple as that. I used to think management actually had our backs, too. I'd go to the summer cookouts they used to throw, I'd stand there eating a hot dog and chatting with the shift supervisors, completely believing we were all on the same team trying to keep the county transit running safely. 

I never looked over my shoulder. I never second-guessed an email. If a supervisor said, "Hey, we're updating this maintenance policy," I just assumed it was for efficiency or because the manufacturer recommended it. I was completely... well, looking back on it now, maybe I was even a little naive, if I'm being completely honest with myself. I just took everything at face value. 

That's what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating, Doc. I wasn't sitting around looking for people to plot against me. I didn't want to find out that they were cutting corners on the brake pads or trying to set me up as the fall guy for their budget deficits. It just... the evidence just piled up right in front of me. You don't have to be a suspicious person to notice when someone is actively trying to sabotage your work week after week. I mean, if a guy is standing outside in a downpour and tells you he's getting wet, you don't ask him if he's always had a suspicious attitude toward the weather, right? He's just getting rained on. And that's me. I'm just dealing with the reality of what's happening in that garage right now. But before this? No. I was an open book. Ask anyone I grew up with. I never had a reason to doubt anybody until they gave me one.
Did this belief that your coworkers were plotting against you come on very suddenly?

Suddenly? Well, no, not like a light switch flipping on, if that's what you mean. It wasn't like I just woke up one Tuesday and thought, "Aha, they're out to get me!" No, it was... it was a slow build, a very gradual thing. It's been going on for about a year now. Yeah, almost exactly a year. 

It all really started right after I got recognized for that county safety initiative. Do you remember me mentioning that? The transit authority had this big push for preventative maintenance, and I caught a series of micro-fractures in the steering columns of the older articulated buses—the 60-footers. It was a big deal. They gave me a plaque, there was a picture in the county newsletter, the whole nine yards. I thought it was a good thing, you know? I thought I was doing my job, keeping the public safe. 

But looking back, that's exactly when the temperature in the room changed. That's when the plot really started taking shape. At first, it was just little things, things you could almost brush off if you weren't paying close attention. Like, my shift assignments would get changed at the last minute, or I'd find my diagnostic tablet uncharged when I specifically remembered plugging it in the night before. Just small inconveniences. I thought it was just administrative incompetence at first. But then, as the months went by—say, around month three or four after the award—it started escalating. 

That's when the procurement guy started questioning my requisition forms. I'd order standard replacement valves, and suddenly it's a whole inquisition about whether I really need them or if I'm "over-maintaining" the fleet. "Over-maintaining"—can you believe that phrase? Like a bus carrying eighty people at highway speeds can be too safe. And then Dave, the shift supervisor, started shadowing me on my walk-arounds, standing just far enough away to pretend he wasn't watching, but I knew he was documenting how much time I spent on each vehicle. 

So, it wasn't sudden at all. It was like watching water come to a boil. It started with the award a year ago—which I now realize put a target on my back because I made management look bad for missing those fractures in the first place—and then it just simmered and simmered, week by week, month by month, with them adding more pressure, more roadblocks, until it became this undeniable, coordinated effort to push me out or set me up to fail. It took a whole year to get to where we are today, Doc. A whole year of them tightening the screws.
Since this started, have you become much less interested in seeing other people or doing things you used to enjoy?

Less interested? No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, my routine hasn't really changed much on that front. I mean, I still get up every morning at 4:30 AM, just like I always have, make my coffee, and I get to work on time. Actually, I'm usually there fifteen minutes early because I like to get a head start before the shift supervisor starts hovering around my bay. 

And my work itself, I'm still completing all my inspections, every single one of them, top to bottom. I don't skip a beat. I'm checking the undercarriages, the fluid levels, the air brakes, everything. I still take a lot of pride in that, maybe even more now because I have to be so thorough. And outside of work, I'm still doing my regular stuff. I still keep up with church every Sunday. I sit in the same section, I talk to the same folks at the fellowship hour afterward. Pastor Thomas even asked me to take a look at the church van's alternator last week, which I did, obviously. And I take care of myself, you know? I keep my apartment clean, I do my laundry, I cook my own meals. I'm not just sitting around in the dark ignoring the world, if that's what
During this past year, have you had a period when your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or unusually irritable for days at a time?

High? Euphoric? No, Doc, definitely not. I mean, why on earth would I be walking around euphoric? If you think about everything I just told you, about what I've been dealing with in that garage for the last twelve months... there's really nothing to be euphoric about, is there? I'm certainly not walking through the depot singing zip-a-dee-doo-dah while they're actively trying to ruin my career and compromise the safety of the county transit system. That wouldn't make any sense at all. 

My mood is just... normal. Well, normal for a guy in my specific situation. You asked about being irritable, too. Now, sure, I get annoyed. I'd be lying if I said I didn't. Like, just last Thursday, I came in and my primary half-inch socket set was pushed all the way to the back of my workbench. It wasn't missing, they didn't steal it, but it was moved just enough to let me know someone had been in my bay messing with my setup. Did that make me irritable? Yes, absolutely it did. But it's not like I'm just flying off the handle for days on end for absolutely no reason, or snapping at the cashier at the grocery store. It's a very specific, completely justified frustration about my workspace being violated. 

And even then, I don't let it consume me for days. Once I re-organize my station and inventory my tools, I just take a deep breath and get back to work. I'm actually a very level-headed guy. I have to be, right? Because if you really think about it, if I start acting erratic, if I start getting too angry or, like you said, unusually high and overly excited, that is exactly what they want. They would use it against me in a heartbeat. Dave would march straight up to HR and say, "Look at him, he's acting unstable, he's a liability in the maintenance bay, we need to pull his inspection credentials." 

So I keep things very, very even. I don't give them that ammunition. I wake up, I come in, I drink my coffee—black, no sugar, same as I've done since I was eighteen—and I just keep my head down and focus on the inspections. I don't have these wild mood swings or days where I'm just buzzing with energy or raging at the world. I'm just steady. I have to stay steady to keep one step ahead of them. So no, none of those weird highs or long angry spells. Just... focused. I'm just very, very focused on making sure the buses are safe and my back is covered.
Have people told you that your facial expression or emotions seem unusually flat or less expressive than before?

Flat? Like... like I don't have any emotions on my face? No, no one has ever said anything like that to me. I mean, I'm not walking around like a zombie or a robot, you know? My face does exactly what it's supposed to do. If something is funny, I laugh. Like the other day, my buddy Mike from the tire bay, he was telling this story about his golden retriever getting stuck in a kiddie pool, and I was cracking up. I was laughing just as hard as anybody else. And if I'm annoyed, like I was telling you earlier about my socket set being moved, I am sure you can see it on my face. I might not scream and shout, but I definitely furrow my brow, you know, I get that look of concentration and frustration. 

Nobody has ever pulled me aside and told me I am looking a little blank lately. If anything, I think I'm very expressive. But, like I was saying before, I do try to keep things professional at the depot. You have to understand, when you know people are documenting your every move, you become very aware of how you present yourself. You do not want to give them the wrong idea. If I walked around with a completely deadpan face all day, staring off into space, well, Dave would probably write that down, wouldn't he? He would put it in his little notebook that the inspector seems disconnected or unresponsive. So I make sure I smile when I say good morning to the security guard at the gate, I make sure I nod and look alert during the safety briefings... I am very engaged. I have to be. So no, definitely not flat. Just... normal. Very normal.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because ever since that county safety award, certain people at work have been twisting my inspection reports and asking pointed budget questions like they’re trying to make me look crooked, and even when my supervisor says it’s just normal review, I can tell there’s a coordinated effort to discredit me.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code.

patient.answer:

I’m a transportation inspector, you know, making sure the county transit vehicles are up to code, checking maintenance logs, all that. And I take my job seriously. I’m good at it. Actually, a little while back, I won this county safety award. It was a big deal, I caught a major brake line issue before it caused a pileup. But, honestly, ever since they handed me that plaque, it’s like... it’s like it put this massive target on my back. 

Certain people at the depot—and I won't name names right this second, but I know exactly who they are—they’ve been taking my inspection reports and completely twisting them around. They pull me aside and ask these incredibly pointed budget questions, scrutinizing every single line item like they’re trying to make me look crooked, like I'm skimming or faking the numbers or something. 

And I went to my supervisor about it, I laid it all out for him, and he just... he brushes it off. He tells me, 'Oh, it’s just a normal review, everyone goes through it, don't worry.' doctor.intent: Differentiate a persistent non-bizarre persecutory delusion without other psychotic symptoms (delusional disorder) from schizophrenia-spectrum disorders by checking for negative symptoms, especially affective flattening.
doctor.question: Have people told you that your facial expression or emotions seem unusually flat or less expressive than before?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about flat affect or reduced emotional expression (negative symptoms of schizophrenia), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Flat? Like... like I don't have any emotions on my face? No, no one has ever said anything like that to me. I mean, I'm not walking around like a zombie or a robot, you know? My face does exactly what it's supposed to do. If something is funny, I laugh. Like the other day, my buddy Mike from the tire bay, he was telling this story about his golden retriever getting stuck in a kiddie pool, and I was cracking up. I was laughing just as hard as anybody else. And if I'm annoyed, like I was telling you earlier about my socket set being moved, I am sure you can see it on my face. I might not scream and shout, but I definitely furrow my brow, you know, I get that look of concentration and frustration. 

Nobody has ever pulled me aside and told me I am looking a little blank lately. If anything, I think I'm very expressive. But, like I was saying before, I do try to keep things professional at the depot. You have to understand, when you know people are documenting your every move, you become very aware of how you present yourself. You do not want to give them the wrong idea. If I walked around with a completely deadpan face all day, staring off into space, well, Dave would probably write that down, wouldn't he? He would put it in his little notebook that the inspector seems disconnected or unresponsive. So I make sure I smile when I say good morning to the security guard at the gate, I make sure I nod and look alert during the safety briefings... I am very engaged. I have to be. So no, definitely not flat. Just... normal. Very normal.

inference.note: Dropped F23 and F20.0: fixed persecutory delusion limited to workplace for ~1 year, no hallucinations, no thought disorder, no negative symptoms, no mood episodes, and functioning largely preserved. Delusional disorder remains most likely; paranoid personality disorder is a lesser differential but premorbid pervasive suspiciousness is denied.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a fixed, highly systematized persecutory belief that coworkers are coordinating to discredit and remove him from work, lasting about one year, with strong conviction and refusal to accept contrary evidence. Psychotic symptoms are otherwise circumscribed: he denies hallucinations, thought insertion/withdrawal, and disorganization, and there is no evidence of prominent mood episodes or negative symptoms. Premorbidly he was not generally suspicious, arguing against a longstanding paranoid personality pattern and supporting delusional disorder, persecutory type.
